title.rendered: Laketown, Fillmore officials get tour of fire facility

content.rendered:
Graafschap Fire Department Chief Doug DenBleyker opened the heavy metal door to the jointly owned live fire training facility at the Saugatuck Township Fire District station, 3342 Blue Star Highway on Monday night, Sept. 28, 2025, for officials from Fillmore and Laketown townships.

The smell of old smoke from the soot-stained walls permeated the cool air as DenBleyker walked officials through the rooms and explained how the facility helps emergency crews safely learn to battle fires.

Outside the three-story structure, Graafschap firefighters prepared for a night of active training.

DenBleyker invited members from the fire board and the boards of the two townships that make up the Graafschap Fire Department so they could see the facility firsthand then watch firefighters in action.

The facility opened in 2019 and is a collaboration of Clyde, Fennville, Ganges, Graafschap, Hamilton, Holland and Saugatuck fire departments and community donations.

Graafschap uses the facility several times a year.

For more information on the Graafschap Fire Department, click here.

title.rendered: State park holds special spot in art celebration

content.rendered:
Saugatuck Dunes State Park in Laketown Township is a special place for the Land Conservancy of West Michigan and for artists Katie Edmiston and Kathy Mohl.

Both artists mixed their talent with brushes and oil paint to capture the natural spirit of the state park and will have their work displayed in the Land Conservancy’s “Preserved! Capturing West Michigan’s Enduring Places” exhibit in October. The Land Conservancy is celebrating 50 years of conservation and asked 16 artists to create art en plein air – in the open, outside — on the group’s protected lands throughout West Michigan.

Proceeds from artwork sales and donations made at the event will benefit the continued protection of West Michigan’s ecologically critical land. The event is 5:30- 9 p.m. Oct. 2 at LaFontsee Galleries, 1504 Plainfield Ave., NE, Grand Rapids.

The paintings will be for sale at the event.

For more information, click here.

A special place

Saugatuck Dunes State Park, 6575 138th Ave., is a significant landmark in the history of the Land Conservancy.

Members of what was then called the Natural Areas Conservancy of West Michigan supported the addition and preservation of 300 acres in the state park almost 40 years ago.

“The volunteers worked with the community to influence the State of Michigan to dedicate money to purchase that property and have it added to Saugatuck Dunes State Park. They also worked to ensure the land was designated as a natural area so that it could not be developed,” said Marie Orttenburger, communication & outreach director of the Land Conservancy of West Michigan. The Saugatuck Dunes Natural Area was dedicated in 1988, and it was later renamed the “Patricia Birkholz Natural Area” in honor of the former state lawmaker who played a key role in its protection.

“It was an important first step, and its success launched the organization into an era of growth. In the years that followed, the Land Conservancy protected its first nature preserve, established an office, and hired its first employees,” she said.

The artists

The two artists tasked with painting the park for the 50th anniversary event said the site is special to them.

Edmiston specifically requested to paint the state park for the Land Conservancy project.

“I visited Saugatuck Dunes and the city of Saugatuck for the first time 11 years ago and was immediately inspired by the landscape and beauty of the natural area,” said Edmiston who lives in Central Michigan.

She is impressed with the park’s diversity of plants and animals.

“From beautiful wildflowers to old-growth forest, to cacti, the park really has it all. This year I was particularly inspired by the ecology of dunes. More than one of my paintings will be focused on the beauty found in different areas of a dune ecological system, including the beach, foredune, and back dunes,” Edmiston said.

Mohl, who lives in Caledonia, has a passion for natural areas and unspoiled landscapes.

“Saugatuck Dunes State Park is one of my absolute favorite places to paint. The dramatic rolling dunes stretching into the distance, the wind-shaped trees and grasses leading to the shores of Lake Michigan create an endlessly inspiring landscape. I feel like I see a painting everywhere I look,” Mohl said.

“It is a place that continually challenges and inspires me as a plein air painter. My work is not simply about recording what a place looks like, I’m expressing how it feels,” she said. “When I’m at the Saugatuck Dunes State Park, I experience a sense of mystery and reverence for the environment. I hope my paintings convey that feeling and invite viewers to experience their own sense of connection to nature. … My work is not simply about recording what a place looks like, I’m expressing how it feels. When I’m at the Saugatuck Dunes State Park, I experience a sense of mystery and reverence for the environment.”

Mohl recalls her first visit to the park in 2017.

“After hiking the beach trail through the woods with all of my painting gear, I caught my first glimpse of the sparkling water through the trees. It felt like I discovered a place that was untouched by development. It was breathtaking. I’ve returned to paint there many times since then,” she said.

Painting challenges

Both artists noted the challenges of painting in the open air at a Lake Michigan park.

Edmiston said part of plein air painting sometimes includes interacting with and adapting to the natural wildlife in the area.

“A horde of sand flies descended on me in the early morning while completing a beach painting, so I improvised long pants out of my painting towel to keep myself from being swarmed. Later that day, I also had to swiftly pack up and relocate my easel after a sparrowhawk decided I had set up too close to her nest, and started divebombing me,” Edmiston said. “It’s all a part of the adventure!”

Mohl said changing weather conditions, including heat and wind, create challenges for outdoor painters.

“The shifting light can dramatically change the colors and overall feeling of a scene, requiring me to make decisions quickly. That constant interaction with nature is what makes plein air painting so rewarding for me. Ticks and sunburn are always a concern so I’m careful to dress appropriately and protect myself,” she said.

Other artists participating in “Preserved!” are:

Betsy Oneill, Carolyn Damstra, Cloe Hadley, Ellie Iorio, Jean Allemeier Boot, Justin Kellner, Kathleen Kalinowski, Kathy Mohl, Katie Edmiston, Lori McElrath Eslick, Lynn Anderson, Michael Pfleghaar, Sally Jenks, Spencer High and Yolanda Gonzalez.

Other Laketown locations

Overall, the Land Conservancy has 165 properties, 13,097 acres, 91 miles of shoreline and serves eight counties, according to its website.

In Laketown Township, the Land Conservancy protects four properties:

  • Castle Park Nature Preserve – 5 acres and 400 feet of Lake Michigan Shoreline.
  • Dune Pines Nature Preserve – 4574 S. Audubon St. 13 acres
  • Huyser Farm Park – 4188 64th St. 102 acres.
  • Saugatuck Dunes State Park – 6575 138th Ave. 1,000 acres

title.rendered: Celebrate July 4th with community pancake breakfast

content.rendered:
Celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary with the 58-year tradition of food and community at the Annual July Fourth Pancake Breakfast at the Graafschap Fire Department, 4534 60th St.

The event is 6-10 a.m. Saturday, July 4. Suggested donation is $6 for adults and $3 for children. All money goes to Friends of the Graafschap Fire Department, a 501(c)(3) organization that sponsors the event and distributes the funds collected to charitable organizations that in the past included Girls on the Run, Great Lakes Kids Burn Camp, Firefighter Cancer Support Network.

“I believe most people attend the breakfast because they want to celebrate our country’s independence with their friends and neighbors,” said Graafschap Fire Department Chief Doug DenBleyker who has attended more than 40 of the pancake breakfasts.

Check out pictures from last year’s event here.

Pancakes, sausage links, coffee, milk and orange juice are on the menu. Fire trucks, equipment and services will be on display along with items for children.

Last year’s event brought in 1,365 people.

Get a quick video tour of last year’s event here.

Sponsors include Biggby Coffee, Dunes View Kwik Shop, Lawrence Towing, Shoreline Container and Packaging, Quincy Street Market, and Republic Services.

The pancake breakfast started in 1968 as a way for the Graafschap Civic Club to raise money for a ball field. The fire department took over organizing and running the breakfast in 1991 to thank the community for its support.

By the numbers

Firefighters have pancake-flipping down to a science and community members dress in their finest red, white and blue for the holiday event.

Here are some more details about the event:

  • Number of chairs: About 400
  • Number of tables: About 60
  • Number of grills: 8
  • Pancake batter used: 300 pounds in 2025
  • Sausages served: 320 pounds
  • Coffee served: About 800 cups (9 pounds of coffee)
  • Orange juice served: 768 single-serve containers.
  • Total number of people served from 2021-2025: 6,211

title.rendered: Fire dept. achieves Premier Blood Partner status

content.rendered:
Graafschap Fire Department has been recognized by the American Red Cross as one of its Premier Blood Partners for 2026 for its support of the community and national blood supply.

Last year, Graafschap Fire Department helped the Red Cross collect 215 blood donations as part of its deep-rooted commitment to help save the lives of patients facing illnesses and injuries in this community and across the country.

“Graafschap Fire Department is proud to be a part of the Red Cross mission that helps ensure lifesaving blood is available for hospital patients in need,” said Capt. Dave Grumney at Graafschap Fire Department. “Our organization shares that same humanitarian value to help our neighbors, and we are grateful for the opportunity to host blood drives that will do just that here in our community.”

The Premier Blood Partners program is for top blood drive partners and offers recognition to the highest contributing sponsors, according to the Red Cross website.

Every day, volunteer blood and platelet donors across the country are needed to help save lives. Blood and platelets are needed for accident and burn victims, heart surgery and organ transplant patients, and those receiving treatment for leukemia, cancer or sickle cell disease, according to the Red Cross.

Graafschap Fire Department started hosting blood drives in 2023.

Next blood drive

Graafschap Fire Department will host a Red Cross blood drive on May 28 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the fire station, 4534 60th St. Community members are urged to come out and roll up a sleeve.

“Blood donations are essential to the health of our community. We encourage those who can join us to give the gift of life. The donation process only takes about an hour and can make an enormous difference for a patient battling illness or injury,” said Grumney.

To schedule an appointment to donate blood at The Graafschap Fire Department, click here or call 1-800-RED-CROSS (1-800-733-2767).

Donors of all blood types are needed. Blood is a perishable product that can only come from volunteer blood donors. 

About the department

Graafschap Fire Department responds to fire, medical and other emergency situations in all of Laketown Township and part of Fillmore Township, and assists other agencies as needed.

The department also takes a proactive approach to prevention, offering free home safety inspections, free blood pressure checks on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to noon at the firehouse, 4534 60th St., and blood drives as part of its Community Risk Reduction Program.

Community Risk Reduction Program efforts totaled 154 hours in 2025 and included school visits, smoke alarm installations, weekly blood pressure screenings, home safety audits, CPR classes, and business pre-plans.

For more information, click here.

title.rendered: Friends of Graafschap Fire Dept. offering scholarship

content.rendered:
The Friends of the Graafschap Fire Department is offering a $500 scholarship to be awarded to a high school senior residing in the Graafschap Fire Department coverage area.

This is the first time the group will award a scholarship.

The application deadline is May 1, 2026, with the recipient notified June 1.

Details

The recipient must be a high school senior who plans to graduate high school and be enrolled in further education that can include tech or trade school, college or university or other post-high school education.

Firefighters hope this scholarship may help someone on their way to being a firefighter.

The recipient must live in the Graafschap Fire Department response area that includes all Laketown Township and parts of Fillmore Township.

For a map of the coverage area, visit here.

Applicants must write and submit a 500- to 750-word essay on these possible topics:

  • What do you plan to do to further your education?
  • How will you use the scholarship award? (Books, tuition, rooming, gas money etc.)
  • What was it like growing up in the area?

Submit essays to davegrumney@graafschapfire.org before the close of business on May 1.

Send any questions to Capt. Dave Grumney at davegrumney@graafschapfire.org or call (616) 396-4060 ext. 703.

About the group

Friends of the Graafschap Fire Department is a 501c non-profit that raises funds through the July Fourth pancake breakfast and from private donors.

Besides the scholarship, the group also disperses funds through Hungry for Christ, Toys for Tots, Shields of Hope, Great Lakes Children’s Burn Camp, Girls on the Run, Firefighter Cancer Support Network and Tunnels to Towers.

title.rendered: Get burn permits through fire department

content.rendered:
You can burn branches and twigs in Laketown Township, but you need a burn permit from the Graafschap Fire Department.

Call the department, (616) 396-4060, on the day you are going to burn or the day before. If there is no answer when you call, please leave a message in the burn permit voice mailbox and we will call you right back. There is no fee for a burn permit. You will receive verbal approval, unless weather and dryness conditions prohibit safe burning.

If you live in a subdivision in Laketown Township, you may burn on odd days only and a permit is required.

You are not permitted to burn such items as treated lumber, construction debris, furniture, appliances or garbage.

title.rendered: No burn permits until rain arrives

content.rendered:
No burn permits will be issued today, Friday, Sept. 19, 2025, or Saturday, Sept. 20, in Laketown Township until the township receives rain.

If you have questions, contact Graafschap Fire Department Chief Doug DenBleyker at (616) 396-4060.

“Much of the Lower Peninsula has only had about two-thirds of normal precipitation totals since January 1. Even more dry weather over the last 30 days has only made things worse,” the National Weather Service in Grand Rapids posted on its Facebook page on Thursday, Sept. 18.  “All of this is adding up to the most significant drought we’ve had in the area since 2012.”

The U.S. Drought Monitor released its weekly report on Thursday, Sept. 18, putting Laketown Township and other parts of northwestern Allegan County, much of Ottawa County and parts of Kent County in the Severe Drought category.

Farmers are reporting diminished yields and early harvests, and river levels are lower than usual, the weather service reported.

“Rain showers are returning to the forecast, but widespread significant rains don’t look likely over the next 1 to 2 weeks, so these dry conditions could continue to worsen,” the agency said.

For more on the drought, visit WOOD TV 8 here.

title.rendered: Take precautions to handle upcoming heat wave

content.rendered:
Laketown Township is included in an extreme heat watch from Saturday morning, June 21, 2025, to Tuesday evening, June 24.

The heat watch includes Allegan, Ottawa and Kent counties. The watch is expected to be elevated to a warning this weekend.

Laketown Township is also included in an Air Quality Advisory for Saturday, June 21, due to elevated levels of ozone.

For more on the weather, visit https://www.weather.gov/grr/

Dangerously hot conditions with heat index values up to 102 degrees are possible. Heat related illnesses increase significantly during extreme heat and high humidity events.

What to do

The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services is urging residents to take steps to protect themselves from risks related to hot weather.

As daily temperatures rise above 80 degrees, emergency room visits for heat-related illness increase, the state agency said in a press release issued today, June 20. This is often more likely early in the summer season as people are not yet used to high temperatures and are not taking the necessary precautions.

To prevent complications from the heat, residents are encouraged to:

  • Drink more fluids and avoid liquids with large amounts of sugar or alcohol.
  • Limit outdoor activities to when it is coolest in the morning and evening.
  • Spend time indoors in air conditioning.
  • Wear lightweight, light-colored and loose-fitting clothing.
  • Wear sunscreen, as sunburn affects a body’s ability to cool down.
  • Check on elderly neighbors and relatives to determine if they need assistance.

In addition to reaching out to Michigan 211 to locate cooling centers, residents can also spend some time at an air-conditioned store, shopping mall or other public building, according to the press release.

In addition to staying hydrated and out of the sun, residents are reminded to never leave children or pets alone in a car even with windows cracked.

For more details from the state on how to handle the hot weather, visit here.

Heat-related illnesses

Heat exhaustion and heatstroke are both forms of heat-related illness. Signs of heat-related illness vary but may include:

Heavy sweating; Muscle cramps; Weakness; Dizziness; Headache; Nausea; Vomiting; Fainting; Extremely high body temperature (above 103°F); and Tiredness.

Heatstroke occurs when the body is unable to regulate its temperature and can result in death if not treated promptly. Humidity can make temperatures feel even hotter and further stress the body’s ability to self-regulate. If you suspect someone has heatstroke, call 911 for immediate medical help and try to cool the person down.

title.rendered: Safety precautions key in cold weather

content.rendered:
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission urges consumers to take safety precautions while keeping their homes warm this winter. Here are some tips provided through the Allegan County Health Department.

Two hazards of special concern are fires and carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which have been linked to home heating equipment used during the colder winter months, including space heaters, furnaces and fireplaces. 

Portable Heaters: TheCPSC estimates that portable heaters, including electric space heaters, are involved in an average of 1,600 fires per year, resulting in an average of 70 deaths and 160 injuries annually from 2019 to 2021.

Portable heaters can cause fires if they are placed too close to combustible materials such as drapes, furniture or bedding, so make sure to place them at least three feet away from these materials.

Other heat sources

Furnaces, fireplaces and chimneys: Have a professional inspect all fuel-burning heating systems, including furnaces, boilers, fireplaces, wood stoves, water heaters, chimneys, flues and vents each year. Fireplaces can cause fires if the chimney is cracked, blocked or coated with creosote, or if sparks and embers reach flammable materials.

Generators: A gasoline-powered generator used during winter weather-related power outages can produce as much CO as hundreds of cars. The CPSC estimates that from 2012-2022, about 750 people died from CO poisoning associated with generators. Never use a generator inside a home, basement, shed or garage.

title.rendered: Graafschap Fire Dept. expanding blood drive dates

content.rendered:
Blood drives at the Graafschap Fire Department station continue to grow in popularity. Starting in January, the American Red Cross drives will happen every other month – six times a year — at the Laketown Township site instead of quarterly — four times a year.

The last quarterly event is Thursday, Nov. 21, 2024, from 10 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. at the station, 4534 60th St.

For an appointment on Nov. 21, visit RedCrossBlood.org and enter sponsor code GFD or call (800) 733-2767.

More dates

Blood drives started at the fire station on Aug. 31, 2023. Each successive quarterly event collected more units. The growing popularity of the drives led organizers to move the collection site from the training room to the larger area in the truck bays.

“The quarterly blood drives at the Graafschap Fire Department have been very successful so far,” said blood drive coordinator Dave Grumney, Captain, Training & Health/Safety at the department. He reached out to the American Red Cross to changing the schedule from quarterly to every other month.

The new arrangement will allow regular donors to fulfill their 56-day rotation.

The scheduled dates are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Thursdays Jan. 30, March 27, May 29 and July 31.

Previously, the fire department drew on the marketing from another drive at Central Wesleyan Church. Now, the department will be on its own to attract donors, with recruitment already beginning for the new schedule.

“When GFD ran under the Central Wesleyan banner, we were able to communicate to all donors affiliated with that drive. Now that they have our own banner, we’ll have to recruit from the ground up,” said Scot Dinsmor, regional coordinator for the American Red Cross. “The good news is that the blood drives will be searchable on the Red Cross website using the donors zip code, but they can also use the sponsor code ‘GraafschapFD.’”

During blood drives at the fire station, donors can meet firefighters, take a tour of the station and have questions answered about other programs including smoke detector checks and installation, rental inspections, burn permits, CPR classes, and home safety audits.

Risk reduction

These programs are a part of the Community Risk Reduction initiative started in 2022.

The department has free weekly blood pressure checks at the facility from 10 a.m. to noon on Wednesdays.

Reflective address signs are made in-house by Graafschap Fire Department retirees. The signs are usually ready for pick up at the fire station after two business days of receiving the order – and the $20 cost is paid at the time of pick-up.

The signs can also be ordered here.

The program also continues a smoke and carbon monoxide installation program. Free alarms installed by firefighters are available to residents. These 10-year lithium battery alarms are provided by a state grant.

For more information, call the fire department at (616) 396-4060 or visit here.

title.rendered: Polls open today until 8 p.m.

content.rendered:
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. today Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024, to choose federal, state and local candidates.

Early in-person voting which ended Nov. 3 saw its highest turnout since the process was first used in February.

Information for today

Laketown Township voters will cast ballots in their regular precincts in today’s election:

Precinct 1 (Holland Public Schools): Laketown Township Hall, 4338 Beeline Road.

Precinct 2 (Hamilton Public Schools): Graafschap Fire Department, 4534 60th St.

Precinct 3 (Saugatuck Public Schools): Laketown Township Hall, 4338 Beeline Road.

For more information on the election, visit laketowntwp.org/elections or call the clerk’s office at (616) 335-3050.

On the ballot

At the federal level, voters will choose a U.S. President, U.S. Senator and U.S. Representative.

At the state level, voters will choose a representative and members of the State Board of Education, University of Michigan Regents, Michigan State University Trustees and Wayne State University Governors.

Judge choices are Judge of the Supreme Court, Judge of Court of Appeals 3rd District, Judge of Circuit Court 48th Circuit, Judge of Circuit Court 48th Circuit (partial term), Judge of District Court 57th District, Judge of Probate Court Allegan County.

Countywide elected positions on the ballot are prosecuting attorney, sheriff, clerk-register of deeds, treasurer, drain commissioner, surveyor and board of commission member.

At the township level, Laketown voters will choose from these candidates on the ballot:

  • Supervisor (Choose 1): Steven Ringelberg (Republican)
  • Clerk (Choose 1): Jim Delaney (Republican)
  • Treasurer (Choose 1): Jim Johnson (Republican); Stacey Lefevre (Independent)
  • Trustee (Choose 2): Mark S. Timmerman (Republican), Michael Koeman (Republican)
  • Parks Commissioner (Choose 5): Thomas Evan Hoekman (Republican), Brad Laninga (Republican), Mary Jo Bertolino (Republican), Sherry Sirko (Republican), Michael Teekamp (Republican)

For voters in Precinct 1 — Holland Public Schools (Choose 2): Liz Colburn, Diane V. Ybarra

For voters in Precinct 2 — Hamilton Public Schools (Choose 3): Loren Joostberns, Candice Dykstra, Janell Simmons

For voters in Precinct 3 — Saugatuck Public Schools: (Choose 4 plus one partial position expiring on Dec. 31, 2026): All will be write-in candidates.

Early voting recap

Early in-person voting was Oct. 26 through Nov. 3 at the township hall. In total, 1,595 people voted early, more than 10 times the number who voted early in person for the August Primary Election and 28.9 percent of all registered voters.

“Our numbers balanced each day. Early voting ballots will get tabulated, counted, and processed after the polls close on Election Day,” said Clerk Amber Davis. “Thank you to all the residents who came out to vote!”

As of Nov. 3, Laketown had 5,513 registered voters.

The first day of early in-person voting on Saturday, Oct. 26, was the most popular with 238 people.

The other days are:

Sunday, Oct. 27 – 116 people
Monday, Oct. 28 – 164 people
Tuesday, Oct. 29 – 144 people
Wednesday, Oct. 30 – 154 people
Thursday, Oct. 31 – 171 people
Friday, Nov. 1 – 220 people
Saturday, Nov. 2 – 170 people
Sunday, Nov. 3 – 218 people.

This election is the third time residents in Laketown Township have been able to vote early. The first time was Feb. 17-25, 2024, for the Presidential Primary. The second time was July 27-Aug. 4, 2024, for General Primary.

In Laketown Township, 173 voters took advantage of early voting in February.

In July-August, 121 voters cast early ballots.

Statewide voters passed Proposal 2 in 2022 to create early in-person voting.

As of Sunday, Nov. 3, Laketown received 1,562 absentee ballots of the 1,750 absentee ballots issued.

Overall, as of Sunday, Nov. 3, about 57.3 percent of registered voters cast ballots through early in-person voting and absentee.

title.rendered: Search committee chooses 3 finalists for manager position

content.rendered:
Laketown Township has narrowed its search for a new manager to three candidates who will return for second interviews on Wednesday, Nov. 6, 2024.

The Laketown Township Manager Search Committee chose Robert Genetski, Brandon Mersman and Karen Sherwood for another round of interviews after about three-and-a-half hours of questions for five total candidates on Wednesday, Oct. 30.

“We are blessed with a rich pool of candidates,” said Supervisor Linda Howell who leads the eight-member search committee.

Other candidates interviewed were Peter Bratt and Andrea Dumbrell.

The three returning candidates will participate in a “meet and greet” event with the public at 1 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 6, at the township hall, 4338 Beeline Road, with interviews beginning at 3 p.m. Each interview is expected to take about 45 minutes. After that, the search committee will discuss which candidate will be offered the manager position. The entire day is open to the public.

The candidates

Genetski is the current Allegan County Clerk and Register of Deeds. The Saugatuck resident has a Master of Education degree from Grand Valley State University and a Bachelor of Arts in English from Auburn University, served in the Governor’s Office of Regulatory Reinvention/Office of the Executive Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs in Lansing, was state representative for the 80th District that included Laketown Township, and was a high school teacher in the at-risk program at Grandville Public Schools.

Mersman is the current city manager of Bronson, Mich. The Bronson resident has a Master of Public Administration degree from Grand Valley State University and a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and Psychology from Hope College. He was assistant to the township manager in Brighton Township, project administrator and grant consultant for the City of Holland, planning and performance improvement office intern at Ottawa County, project administrator management intern for the City of Holland and project administrator management intern for the Village of Spring Lake.

Sherwood is the current assistant manager/human resources director for Grand Haven Charter Township. The Saugatuck resident has a Doctor of Philosophy degree from Eastern Michigan University, a Master of Art degree in Educational Leadership from Grand Valley State University, a Master of Art degree in Early Childhood Education from Central Michigan University and a Bachelor of Art degree in Elementary Education from the University of Michigan. She was deputy superintendent of human resources for Holland Public Schools, superintendent of Kalkaska Public Schools, superintendent of Boyne Falls Public Schools, middle school principal at Boyne City Public Schools and a teacher in various districts.

On Oct. 30, each candidate was asked the same 18 questions by Howell. Questions included why they are interested in the manager position, their communication styles, budget and financial experience, grants, transparency and zoning and code enforcement.

The candidates also directed questions to the search committee.

The process

Current Manager Al Meshkin announced in July his plans to retire Jan. 3, 2025. He has been manager for 35 years. The board hired the firm MGT in August for a cost of about $25,000 to conduct the search for his replacement.

Earlier this month, the township board established a Manager Search Committee consisting of the five-member township board plus three residents who won positions in the Republican primary on Aug. 6. Those three will go on to the Nov. 5 General Election but face no competition.

They are Steven Ringelberg who is running unopposed for the position of supervisor, and Michael Koeman and Mark Timmerman who are running unopposed for trustee positions.

The search committee chose the five candidates on Oct. 23 from a field of about 40 applicants that was narrowed to 11.

Trustee Jim Delaney was not present at the Oct. 23 or Oct. 30 meetings.

title.rendered: Early in-person voting starts on Saturday

content.rendered:
Polls will open for early voting on Saturday, Oct. 26, to Sunday, Nov. 3, at Laketown Township Hall, 4338 Beeline Road.

Even if you normally vote at the Graafschap Fire Station (Precinct 2), you will early vote at the township hall.

Early voting is 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily.

For samples of ballots and more information, visit laketowntwp.org/elections or call the clerk’s office at (616) 335-3050.

The polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5.

This is the third time residents in Laketown Township have been able to vote early. The first time was Feb. 17-25, 2024, for the Presidential Primary. The second time was July 27-Aug. 4, 2024, for General Primary.

In Laketown Township, 173 voters took advantage of early voting in February.

In July-August, 121 voters cast early ballots.

Statewide voters passed Proposal 2 in 2022 to create early in-person voting.

Absentee ballots

The deadline to submit an application to request an absentee ballot be mailed to you is Friday, Nov. 1, at 5 p.m. All ballots must be signed by the voter and returned no later than Tuesday, Nov. 5, at 8 p.m. to be tabulated. The cost of return postage has been paid and there is no charge to the voter.

As of Friday, Oct. 18, there were 1,709 absentee ballots mailed out and 917 returned.

In the 2020 Presidential Election, 2,565 people voted by absentee ballots.

Overall turnout

Laketown Township traditionally exceeds the county average in voter turnout and ranks at the top among local municipalities.

In the 2020 Presidential Election, Laketown’s turnout was 82.8 percent of registered voters. Allegan County overall had a turnout rate of 76.24 percent.

Voters in Laketown Township have candidates and issues to choose from on the ballot in the Nov. 5 election.

At the federal level, voters will choose a U.S. President, U.S. Senator and U.S. Representative at the federal level.

At the state level, voters will choose a representative and members of the State Board of Education, University of Michigan Regents, Michigan State University Trustees and Wayne State University Governors.

Judge choices are Judge of the Supreme Court, Judge of Court of Appeals 3rd District, Judge of Circuit Court 48th Circuit, Judge of Circuit Court 48th Circuit (partial term), Judge of District Court 57th District, Judge of Probate Court Allegan County.

Countywide elected positions on the ballot are prosecuting attorney, sheriff, clerk-register of deeds, treasurer, drain commissioner, surveyor and board of commission member.

At the township level, Laketown voters will choose from these candidates on the ballot:

  • Supervisor (Choose 1): Steven Ringelberg (Republican)
  • Clerk (Choose 1): Jim Delaney (Republican)
  • Treasurer (Choose 1): Jim Johnson (Republican); Stacey Lefevre (Independent)
  • Trustee (Choose 2): Mark S. Timmerman (Republican), Michael Koeman (Republican)

For voters in Precinct 1 — Holland Public Schools (Choose 2): Liz Colburn, Diane V. Ybarra

title.rendered: Audit shows Laketown in strong financial health

content.rendered:
Laketown Township is in solid financial condition, according to its recently completed audit.

Joshua Gabrielse, CPA and principal of Siegfried Crandall PC, presented the 2023-2024 fiscal year audit to the township board on Wednesday, July 10, 2024.

Click here for a copy of the audit.

Highlights from the report include:

  • The township’s total net position increased by $486,095 (6 percent) as a result of the year’s activity;
  • Of the $9,375,078 in total net position reported, $1,296,105 (14 percent) is available to be used to meet the township’s ongoing obligations without constraints established by debt covenants, enabling legislation or other legal requirements;
  • The general fund’s unassigned fund balance at the end of the fiscal year was $1,464,070, representing 87 percent of general fund expenditures. “That’s a really good position to be in,” Gabrielse said. The almost $1.5 million fund balance could sustain township operations for about 10-and-a-half months.

Township Manager Al Meshkin asked Gabrielse to summarize how the township stands financially.

“I would say average to excellent,” he responded.

The audit also noted the township has $491,744 in long-term debt, a decrease of $169,990 due to timely principal payments. The board has been making several early payments on bonds including the Felt Estate.

The Fiscal Year 2024-2025 budget does not anticipate significant changes in revenue sources.

“The township has budgeted expenditures for the upcoming year at amounts sufficient to support its ongoing programs and activities, while maintaining the current levels of its resources,” the report said.

When asked if there were areas in the audit the township could improve upon, Gabrielse replied, “No.”

He said Meshkin and the township staff were easy to work with and the quality of the books were “extremely easy” to look at.

The township’s fiscal year is April 1 through March 31.

The township board approved its 2024-2025 budget in March. The current budget increases the end-of-year fund balance by about $5,000 over the previous year’s budget.

At Wednesday’s meeting, the board unanimously approved amendments to this year’s budget, mainly to move the funds from last year to this year for the demolition of the Huyser House.

Supervisor Linda Howell was absent from Wednesday’s meeting.

In other business, the township board:

  • Accepted the retirement letter from Meshkin. His last day is Jan. 3, 2025. He has served the township for 35 years.
  • Approved seeking full-service recruitment proposals to assist with the search for the next manager. Meshkin said proposals should be returned for action at the August meeting with a replacement chosen by the end of the year “for a seamless transition,” he said.
  • Approved an amendment to the recently passed open burning ordinance. The changes better define recreational fires and give the Graafschap Fire Department chief more authority over permitting in the dune areas west of 66th Street.

title.rendered: Hundreds celebrate at pancake breakfast

content.rendered:
Some came by car, by truck or by scooter to the annual Graafschap Fire Department Pancake Breakfast on Thursday, July 4, 2024. Others came by bike, by motorcycle or wagon pulled by a tractor. And Al Davis even walked through in his birthday suit, perfectly comfortable among the hundreds of people inside the fire station at 4534 60th St. in Laketown Township.

His attire was red, white and blue and star-spangled from head to toe to celebrate the birth of America’s independence.

“It’s a birthday suit,” he said as he sat down with Deb Wiersma to enjoy the pancakes and sausage.

Firefighters and family flipped the flapjacks, sizzled the sausage and refilled water and coffee cups as the line looped through the garage, down the driveway and along the street. Fire trucks and apparatus were on display and booths offered information on fire safety, cardiopulmonary resuscitation classes, green address signs and recruiting information.

The breakfast is a way to thank the community for the trust they have placed in the department and their support of the fire millages that fund the department, Fire Chief Doug DenBleyker said.

Donations were also collected and given to charities including Girls on the Run that teaches essential life skills with a blend of physical activity; Great Lakes Burn Camp at Pretty Lake Camp in Mattawan that promotes healing, self-esteem, confidence and general well-being for burn injured children; Tunnel to Towers Foundation that provides mortgage-free homes to Gold Star and fallen first responder families with young children and specially adapted smart homes for catastrophically injured veterans and first responders; Firefighter Cancer Support Network that provides assistance to cancer-stricken firefighters and their families; and Marine Corps Toys for Tots that provides toys, books and emotional support to children.

History

The pancake breakfast started in 1968 as a way for the Graafschap Civic Club to raise money for a ball field. The fire department took over organizing and running the breakfast in 1991.

Last year’s event drew 1,265 to the fire station and raised $7,200.

The Graafschap Fire Department serves all of Laketown Township and part of Fillmore Township.  For more information, visit the fire department’s website.

title.rendered: Board OKs appeal to Open Burning ordinance

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township Board of Trustees on Wednesday, June 12, 2024, unanimously approved the first appeal to the township’s new Open Burning ordinance. The appeal could lead to a change in the rules that gives more authority to the fire chief to decide who can burn brush west of 66th Street.

Supervisor Linda Howell instructed the original burn ordinance committee to draft changes to the rules and report back to the township board.

The ordinance

The township looked at the rules around open burning for about six months and set up a committee to look at changes. Trustees Patrick Dietrich and Jim Delaney worked with Graafschap Fire Chief Doug DenBleyker with input from residents to come up with the new rules.

The ordinance, which went into effect in May, divides fires into recreational and open burning categories.

A recreational fire is a small outdoor fire used for cooking, warming or a social gathering. The rules permit recreational fires west of 66th Street with yearly approval from the fire department who will inspect containers used for fire.

Even with the approval, those who want to burn must still call each time for a burn permit.

Open burning is a fire from which the combustion emissions pass directly into the open air without first passing through a stack or chimney. Open burning fires can include brush, limbs, and stumps. Open burning requires a permit and is allowed in the township but not west of 66th Street unless approved through an appeal process with the township board.

Appeal

Paul Denhartigh, 4604 66th St., has been open burning for the last 7 years on his property, but the new ordinance changed that. He asked to be allowed to continue to open burn.

“Our property happens to be immediately west of 66th street, however, it is not in the Lake Michigan Shore and Dune Area,’’ Denhartigh wrote in a letter to the board.

The concern over safety stems from a 2007 fire in the dunes that destroyed homes and property.

Denhartigh’s land has easy access with two paved roads and has fire hydrants nearby.

“We understand the desire for an easily definable line of demarcation, however, we feel that we have been inadvertently caught in the crosshairs, and have become ‘collateral damage’ because of an arbitrary line, which doesn’t take into consideration property characteristics and we believe is inconsistent with the intent/purpose of this ordinance,” he said.

Board members agreed and granted Denhartigh’s appeal.

Other business

In other business, the board unanimously:

  • Approved a resolution to proceed with the assessor’s plat for a portion of Macatawa Park for cottages along the south side of Griswold Avenue. The project will define property borders. There will be no cost to township taxpayers.
  • Approved the appointment of Jay Cravens to fill the remaining term of Richard Becker on the planning commission. The term expires Dec. 31, 2026.
  • Approved the Laketown Township Parks and Recreation Commission Community Recreation Plan that will help the parks commission apply for grants.
  • Approved a zoning map amendment Ordinance No. 210 to rezone two parcels on Blue Star Highway from C-1 Neighborhood Business District to Multi-Use District. The planning commission approved the change on May 1.

title.rendered: Board approves funds for community services

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township Board of Trustees approved funds for services from area community groups on Wednesday, June 12, 2024.

“We are not an island with a moat around us,” said Supervisor Linda Howell about the contracted services. “We’re part of a community.”

The board voted 3-2 to allocate $17,000 in funds to the following groups:

Evergreen Commons (a place for older adults to live active lives) — $4,000; Holland American Legion Band — $500; Holland Fireworks — $1,775; Seventy X Seven (restoring the lives of people affected by incarceration) — $1,000; Resilience (formerly known as the Center for Women in Transition) — $2,000; Reach for Recovery (helps recovering addicts) – $1,000; Allegan County Legal Assistance (helps with civil issues including divorce, personal protection, child support, landlord-tenant and guardianship) — $1,725; Holland Chorale — $500; Escape Ministries (intervenes in the lives of youth who fall through the cracks) — $2,000; Holland Symphony — $500; FellinLove Farm (a family farm in Laketown Township for all ages and abilities) — $2,000.

Board discussion

Clerk Amber Davis introduced on Wednesday her suggestion for funding which lowered some payments and increased others from the original proposal. FellinLove Farm, for example, increased from $1,000 to $2,000 while Evergreen Commons dropped from $5,000 to $4,000. Her proposal ultimately passed.

She said the township cannot directly provide the services these groups offer.

“By supporting these, we’re supporting our residents,” she said.

Trustee Patrick Dietrich, who supported the final vote, was concerned about the overall cost and that the money could be spent on other township issues, such as fire department funding.

“I would just like to save a few dollars,” he said.

Overall, the board is spending $1,000 less than the original $18,000 proposal made by township Manager Al Meshkin. The township has been paying for these contracted services for many years.

If the township allocates these funds next year, Dietrich said the distribution should be based on need.

Contracts

Treasurer Jim Johnson, who voted against the funding, struggled with the issue, saying the contracts “feel like a donation,” something townships are not allowed by law to do.

All the groups who receive money have individual contracts approved by the township attorney. The contracts spell out what services are supplied to township residents, something that is legal.

Johnson said other communities do not have as many contracted services as Laketown does.

Trustee Jim Delaney opposed the motion as well. He said the group FellinLove Farm should get money from Laketown’s American Rescue Plan Act distribution.

The township contributed $50,000 in ARPA funds in December 2023 to the Community Enhancement Program, a group that distributes grants that support the common good in the community. Groups can apply for the money. The CEP is part of the Macatawa Area Coordinating Committee. Laketown is a member along with Holland and Zeeland cities and Fillmore, Holland, Olive, Park, Port Sheldon and Zeeland townships.

In March, the board agreed to have the groups requesting money make presentations to the board in April and May.

title.rendered: Pancake breakfast brings community together

Donations will be collected and given to charities including Girls on the Run that teaches essential life skills with a blend of physical activity; Great Lakes Burn Camp at Pretty Lake Camp in Mattawan that promotes healing, self-esteem, confidence and general well-being for burn injured children; Tunnel to Towers Foundation that provides mortgage-free homes to Gold Star and fallen first responder families with young children and specially adapted smart homes for catastrophically injured veterans and first responders; Firefighter Cancer Support Network that provides assistance to cancer-stricken firefighters and their families; and Marine Corps Toys for Tots that provides toys, books and emotional support to children.

History

The pancake breakfast started in 1968 as a way for the Graafschap Civic Club to raise money for a ball field. The fire department took over organizing and running the breakfast in 1991.

Last year’s event drew 1,265 to the fire station and raised $7,200.

title.rendered: Township hall closing early Friday

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township office, 4338 Beeline Road, will close at noon on Friday, May 10. The office will reopen for normal operation on Monday, May 13, at 7:30 a.m.

The closure is due to the installation of a new generator. Power will be out at the hall that afternoon. Telephones will not be operational when the power is out.

title.rendered: Township refines outdoor burning ordinance

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township Board of Trustees unanimously approved changes to the township burning ordinance on Wednesday, April 11, 2024, that will allow people to enjoy recreational fires and make sure those fires remain safe, especially in areas with short-term rentals.

The ordinance will go into effect in May after publication in The Holland Sentinel.

The township has been looking at the rules around open burning for about six months and set up a committee to look into possible changes. Trustees Patrick Dietrich and Jim Delaney worked with Graafschap Fire Chief Doug DenBleyker with input from residents who have been split on the rules.

Dietrich called coming up with the new ordinance “threading a needle.”

“If no one’s happy, you probably achieved some level of success,” he said.

“I do appreciate all the work,” said Supervisor Linda Howell.

Recreational fires

The old ordinance did not differentiate between fires for recreation and fires to get rid of debris.

The new ordinance defines a recreational fire as a small outdoor fire used for cooking, warming or a social gathering but it cannot be more than 3 feet in width and it must be in an approved container with a spark-arresting screen having no opening larger than a quarter inch.

The rules permit recreational fires west of 66th Street with yearly approval from the fire department who will inspect containers used for fire.

Open burning

The new ordinance defines open burning as a fire from which the combustion emissions pass directly into the open air without first passing through a stack or chimney. Open burning fires can include brush, limbs, and stumps. Open burning still requires a permit that can be obtained from the fire department or township hall.

Open burning is permitted in the township but not west of 66th Street, according to the new ordinance.

The concern over safety stems from a 2007 fire in the dunes that destroyed homes and property. Battling blazes in the dunes is difficult for the fire department.

The new ordinance makes the person starting or maintaining a fire responsible for all fire suppression costs, liability and damages resulting from the fire.

Short-term rentals

The new ordinance also specifically addresses recreational fires at short-term rental units.

The new rules say rental units must receive an annual Recreational Residential Burning Permit from the fire department. Containers must be inspected and approved by the fire department.

The township may revoke any rental certificate after consideration of the number, character and severity of violations, according to the new ordinance.

title.rendered: Parks commission sets up committees to look at beach issues

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township Parks and Recreation Commission set up two committees to look at parking and environmental issues at Laketown Beach.

The commission is also seeking township residents to serve on the groups.

The committees

At the Wednesday, March 20, 2024, meeting, the parks commission established a Parking Committee and a Dunes Committee.

The Parking Committee will look at the parking situation at the beach, 6710 142nd Ave. Vehicles are limited to parking along the road in designated spots. Area residents have said the number of vehicles creates unsafe situations. Parks Commissioner Tom Hoekman will lead this group. Members will include neighbors, a representative from the Allegan County Sheriff’s Department and other community members.

The Dunes Committee will examine the ecology at the beach as well as stairs and beach access. Parks Commissioner Anne Brand will lead this group. Members will include experts from Hope College and the Outdoor Discovery Center, a representative from a company that could provide new stairs for the beach and community members.

Grass planting to stabilize the dunes is underway at the park. The commission has looked at EZ Beach Steps, adjustable aluminum ready-to-install steps, to replace the current wooden steps. No decision has been made if those new steps will be used.

Other than the experts, the committees will only take Laketown Township residents as members.

Commissioner Dick Becker asked that the committees consider restroom upgrades.

“Keep that on the back burner,” he said.

There is no timeline for the groups though they could start meeting in the next few months, according to Brand.

Other business

In other business, the commission:

  • Agreed to hold a public hearing May 15 on the proposed 2024 Community Parks and Recreation Plan. From there, the plan, which can help the commission acquire grants, will go to the township board for approval.
  • Approved “open play” pickleball times for 8:30 to 11:30 a.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Open play helps people find others to enjoy the game with. A private group will coordinate the play and create a sign explaining the process.
  • Agreed to invite a representative from the Outdoor Discovery Center to discuss programs in township parks. The Outdoor Discovery Center and parks commission partner for multiple programs such as wildflowers walks, frog catching and blueberry picking in township parks.

title.rendered: Township looks to increase board of review pay

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township Board of Trustees is expected to continue with its pay adjustments, increasing compensation for board of review members by 50 percent.

“It’s a very difficult job,” Manager Al Meshkin told the board of trustees at the Wednesday, March 6, workshop meeting.

The board of review hears taxpayer reviews.

The Laketown Township Board of Review is made up of three members: Chairperson Kevin Stoike, Helen Heneveld and Barb Hibiske.

The board of review members now make $20 an hour – “very low when you consider the service they do for the township,” said Meshkin. “It is a difficult and typically thankless job.”

Members must also take state training courses. Starting in 2022, board of review members are required to complete training at least once every two years.

The township board is considering raising the pay from $20 to $30 an hour and will decide the issue at the March 13 regular meeting. Meshkin has asked the pay increase be effective March 1 so members receive pay for this tax season.

The board of review meets Monday, March 11, from 2-5 p.m. and 6 to 9 p.m.; and Tuesday, March 12, from 8 a.m. to noon and 1-3 p.m. at the township hall, 4338 Beeline Road.

To make an appointment, call (616) 335-3050 or email Heather@laketowntwp.org.

Other pay increases

In February, the board of trustees approved pay increases for the parks commission, planning commission, zoning board of appeals and fire board.

Board members received a $15-per-meeting increase and chairpersons received a $25-per-meeting increase.

The current pay is $85 per meeting for a board member and $100 per meeting for a chairperson. It was last increased in 2021.

The new pay is $100 per meeting for a board member and $125 per meeting for a chairperson.

On Jan. 10, the township board approved 3 percent raises for its own members. The clerk received the 3 percent increase plus $10,000 for elections. The township board is paid an annual salary while the other boards and commissions are paid by the meeting.

In other business on March 6, the township board:

  • Agreed to further research a proposed open burning ordinance. The township has been looking at how to handle recreational fires, especially west of 66th Street in difficult-to-access dune areas.
  • Agreed to ask the parks commission to update bid requests to paint and caulk the Old Township Hall, 6280 142nd Ave.
  • Agreed to put demolition bids for the Huyser House, 4158 64th St., on the agenda for the March 13 meeting.

title.rendered: Board OKs salary increases, more for clerk due to elections

content.rendered:
The Laketown Township board on Wednesday, Jan. 10, unanimously approved 3 percent pay increases for its members with an extra $10,000 for the clerk because of expanded election duties.

The township is required to set its salaries at the beginning of the year.

The increases go into effect for the next fiscal year that begins April 1.

The salaries for the two trustees were increased from $5,000 to $5,150 a year for each.

The salary for the treasurer and supervisor were increased from $16,500 to $16,995 a year for each.

The clerk’s salary increased from $16,500 to $16,995 plus $10,000 for a total of $26,995.

Early voting

The increase for the clerk is due to the added election duties with early voting that begins next month for the Feb. 27 Presidential Primary.

Early voting gives residents the opportunity to cast their vote in person nine days prior to the election. All early in-person voting will be at the Laketown Township Hall, 4338 Beeline Road. This is a change for some people who would normally vote in another precinct.

Early in-person voting is 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on the following days: Saturday, Feb. 17; Sunday, Feb. 18; Monday, Feb. 19; Tuesday, Feb. 20; Wednesday, Feb. 21; Thursday, Feb. 22; Friday, Feb. 23; Saturday, Feb. 24; and Sunday, Feb. 25.

For more information on early voting, absentee voting or any other election issue, please contact the clerk’s office at (616) 335-3050 or visit www.laketowntwp.org and click on “Elections & Voting.”

Other business

In other business, the township board:

  • Unanimously approved Poverty Exemptions Guidelines for property taxes. Residents who meet income and asset levels can submit their request to the March Board of Review. “Poverty exemptions are quite rare in our township, but do exist, and have been submitted in the past to the Board of Review,” Laketown Board of Review members wrote in a letter to the board of trustees in 2023. No exemption requests were submitted for the 2023 Board of Review. For more information, contact Laketown Township Assessor Heather Jahr at (616) 335-3050.
  • Unanimously agreed to table discussion on a revised open burning ordinance after the board received more correspondence from residents about the issue.

title.rendered: Free radon test kits at Allegan County libraries

content.rendered:
Free radon test kits are available through January at libraries in Allegan County.

Saugatuck-Douglas District Library, 174 Center St., and Fennville District Library, 400 W. Main St., are participating in the program being handled by the Allegan County Health Department. The free test kits are available while supplies last.

January is Radon Action Month, and the Allegan County Health Department recommends residents to learn more about radon, test for radon levels within their homes, and reduce radon levels within their homes if found. 

What is radon?

Radon is an odorless, tasteless gas that is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. When you breathe in radon, radioactive particles from the decay of radon gas can get trapped in your lungs. It takes many years for lung cancer to develop.  Most people don’t have symptoms until lung cancer is advanced. 

All outdoor and indoor air has some radon in it. Radon can build up in the air in any home or building. According to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS), one in four homes have high levels of radon. Testing is the only way to know if radon levels in your home are high.

Other libraries

Other participating libraries include:

Dorr Township Library, 1804 Sunset Drive, Dorr; Henika District Library, 149 S. Main St. Wayland; Hopkins District Library, 118 E. Main S., Hopkins; Leighton Township Library, 4451 12th St., Wayland; Salem Township Library, 3007 142nd Ave., Burnips; and Ransom District Library, 180 S. Sherwood Ave., Plainwell.

For more information on radon, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at www.cdc.gov or Michigan Department of Health and Human Services at www.michigan.gov/egle.

title.rendered: Community invited to fire department July Fourth pancake breakfast

content.rendered:
The Graafschap Fire Department wants everyone to have a great time at the traditional July Fourth Pancake Breakfast, but along with the pancakes, sausage, orange juice, milk and coffee, the firefighters want you to think about the future of the department.

The pancake breakfast is 6 to 10 a.m. on Tuesday, July 4, at the fire station, 4534 60th St.

Organizers are asking for a $6 donation for adults and $3 donation for children.

Staffing needs

“We’re looking ahead to the future staffing needs of the department,” said Chief Doug DenBleyker. “We are past the point of needing more firefighters and have been trying for several years to increase the number of paid-on-call staff with little success.”

The pandemic reset people’s lives and changed the way they look at their time and how they spend it.

“We are trying to hold on as long as possible utilizing paid-on-call firefighters to provide the services the public expects, but the time is drawing near where we will need to add more full-time staff if paid-on-call numbers do not increase,” he said.

Staffing has dropped over the years – from a recent high of 24 people in 2018 to 15 firefighters today — while calls have increased from 375 in 2012 to 894 in 2022.

At this year’s Pancake Breakfast, the fire department is mixing in a little sample of the firefighter job with the flapjacks and syrup in hopes of getting more recruits.

“During this year’s breakfast we plan to share the benefits, pay and other perks of the job on information posters around the station,” he said.

Helping out

The Pancake Breakfast started in 1968 as a way for the Graafschap Civic Club to raise money for a ball field. The fire department took over organizing and running the breakfast in 1991.

“The event is for the people; it is their fire department. The breakfast is a great way for us to showcase the equipment they have purchased for us to use to protect their lives and property,” said DenBleyker. “The event is also a great way for the residents to build relationships with the firefighters in a non-emergency situation.”

Last year’s event drew 1,406 people and raised about $7,400. In 2021, the event brought in 850 people and raised $4,679.

In the past, the money raised has helped pay for furniture and kitchen appliances at the station and apparel and equipment for the firefighters. It has also been donated to area charities including Hungry for Christ, Shields of Hope, Girls on the Run, Firefighter Cancer Support Network, Tunnel to Towers and The Kids Burn Camp.

Graafschap Fire Department services all of Laketown Township and the western half of Fillmore Township.

title.rendered: UPDATE: Burn ban continues through weekend

content.rendered:
The burn ban in Laketown Township remains in effect at least through the weekend (June 3-4) despite the brief rain received on Thursday.

The ban also includes the area of Fillmore Township covered by the Graafschap Fire Department.

No permits will be issued until the area receives adequate rain.

The National Weather Service in Grand Rapids does have a chance of rain for Saturday.

May was the second driest on record for Grand Rapids, according to WOOD TV 8.

Holland received 1.03 inches of rain for the month. The area usually receives about 4.01 inches of rain in May, according to records.

Getting a burn permit

Burn permits are required for any open fires in Laketown Township. The area west of 66th Street is not allowed to have open fires unless permission is granted by the fire chief or his designee.

Permits can be obtained by calling the fire station at (616) 396-4060 or the township office at (616) 335-3050 during regular business hours. During non-business hours, contact Chief Doug DenBleyker at (616) 218-3227 or Deputy Fire Chief Mike Capel at (616) 886-9232.

For more information on burn permits, see the township ordinances Chapter 16, Article III, Sec. 16, at  https://bit.ly/3quymks

title.rendered: Burn ban remains in effect, few chances of rain

content.rendered:
A burn ban remains in effect for Laketown Township and the area of Fillmore Township covered by the Graafschap Fire Department.

The ban was first put in place before the Memorial Day holiday weekend.

No substantial rain is expected through the weekend, though some scattered showers are forecast for today and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service in Grand Rapids.

Little rain

This May could be the driest since 1987, according to WZZM.

“Fire weather concerns will remain higher than usual through the weekend,” the weather service wrote on its website regarding conditions Thursday through Tuesday. “Slightly less-dry air may flow through on Saturday, though winds may be a little breezier on both Saturday and Sunday. Somewhat cooler (less hot) air may move through on Sunday, but it could be very dry again.”

The Department of Natural Resources is not permitting any open burning from Muskegon, Newaygo and Mecosta counties north through the Upper Peninsula.

Allegan County is in both a very high and extreme risk categories for wildfires, Allegan County Emergency Management said in a Facebook post on Tuesday.

When the fire danger is very high, fires will start easily from most causes. The fires will spread rapidly and have a quick increase in intensity, right after ignition. Small fires can quickly become large fires and exhibit extreme intensity.

When the fire danger is extreme, fires of all types start quickly and burn intensely. All fires are potentially serious and can spread very quickly with intense burning.

Laketown permits

Burn permits are required for any open fires in Laketown Township. The area west of 66th Street is not allowed to have open fires unless permission is granted by the fire chief or his designee.

Normally, permits can be obtained by calling the fire station at (616) 396-4060 or the township office at (616) 335-3050 during regular business hours. During non-business hours, contact Chief Doug DenBleyker at (616) 218-3227 or Deputy Fire Chief Mike Capel at (616) 886-9232.
